summary: Describes how the RFC Series and the RFC Editor function are organized, with community involvement and accountability as the Internet technical community grew. It lays out the framework that lets the series keep fulfilling its purpose as the publisher of Internet technical documents. It is informational and was later replaced by RFC 8729.

eli5.summary: The RFC Series is like a big library of Internet instruction books. This note explains who runs the library, who decides what goes on the shelves, and how everyone gets a say.

questions: how is the rfc series run
what is the independent submission stream
subtitle: The IAB's framework for who runs the RFC Series, who approves documents, and how the rules can change.

tldr.problem: As the Internet community grew, it was unclear who decides what for the RFC Series, and where the IETF, the IAB, the RFC Editor and independent authors each have a say.
tldr.mechanism: The IAB sets out roles for the RFC Editor, the IAB and the IETF Administrative Support Activity, and splits the series into four streams, each with its own approval process and a shared set of publication requirements.
tldr.outcome: The RFC Series gets a clear, accountable framework. This document is Informational and was later obsoleted by RFC 8729 and updated by RFC 5741.

today: RFC 4844 is Informational and has been obsoleted by RFC 8729 and updated by RFC 5741, so those are the documents to read for the current framework.

sections.title: Why the Series Needed a Framework
sections.content:
The first RFC was published in April of 1969. Since then the RFC Series has been the archival series for Internet technical specifications, covering both general contributions from the research and engineering community and standards documents.

As the IETF grew, its needs for archival publication became more rigorous, and the wider community asked for more openness and accountability. The RFC says the series needs a balance of expert implementation, clear management and direction, and appropriate community input.

There was also confusion and tension over where to take issues that affect one group (the IETF, the IAB or independent individuals) versus the whole series. Topics such as intellectual property rights and labeling are examples that must be handled series-wide or not at all. This document is the IAB's answer: a framework, not a new standard.

The mission is stated plainly: the RFC Series is the archival series dedicated to documenting Internet technical specifications, including general contributions from the Internet research and engineering community as well as standards documents. RFCs are available free of charge to anyone via the Internet.
sections.eli5: Lots of different groups were adding books to the same library, and nobody was sure who got to decide what. This note draws up clear rules so everyone knows their part, and the library stays free for anybody to read.

sections.title: Roles and Responsibilities
sections.content:
The RFC Editor began as a single person. Because the work grew, the term now covers a collection of experts and organizations. The RFC Editor is the expert technical editor and series editor, handles editorial management in accordance with the defined processes, and is expected to lead discussions about policies for editing, publishing and archiving.

The IAB has no comprehensive publishing expertise, so its job is to make sure principles are met, the right communities are consulted, and the RFC Editor has what it needs. It approves the appointment of the RFC Editor and the general policy the RFC Editor follows.

The IETF Administrative Support Activity (IASA, from BCP 101) provides funding and operational oversight. The IAOC is its oversight board and the IAD is its chief actor. The IAOC works with the IAB to find suitable persons or entities, and makes contractual agreements with them. The IAB monitors how well the policies work and, in the event of serious non-conformance, may require the IAOC to vary or terminate and renegotiate the arrangements.
sections.eli5: The librarian runs the shelves. A board of advisors picks the librarian and checks the rules are fair, and a business office pays the bills and watches that the work gets done.

sections.title: The Four-Part Framework
sections.content:
The framework supports the operation of the series through public process and definition documents, with clear responsibilities and ways to change them. The RFC Editor is responsible for operations, and the IAB verifies that community input was sought whenever something changes.

It covers four kinds of activity, and for each the RFC gives a definition, who implements it, how it can change, and which documents already apply:

  • Document approval: each stream has its own approval process. The RFC Editor approves documents in only one stream, the Independent Submission stream.
  • Editing, processing and publication: requirements live in community-approved documents. Concrete values are set in agreements between the IASA and the RFC Editor, such as contracts and service level agreements.
  • Archiving, indexing and accessibility: there should be uniform archiving and indexing across all streams. No community document describes this yet, so the archive continues as built by the RFC Editors since the series began.
  • Series-wide guidelines and rules: uniform style and content, including acceptable language, use of references and copyright rules. Existing documents include RFC 2223 on instructions to authors, RFC 3978 and RFC 4748 on copyright, and RFC 3967 and RFC 4897 on normative references.

For every kind of change, the pattern is the same: the IAB works with the RFC Editor to get community input and approves changes by validating that community requirements were properly considered.
sections.eli5: There are four jobs: deciding which books are allowed in, printing them, storing and finding them, and keeping every book in the same style. Each job has a named owner and a fair way to change the rules.

sections.title: The Four RFC Streams
sections.content:
RFCs come from several communities, each with its own approval process. The RFC calls these streams. Naming them is not meant to divide the series. It is meant to reduce friction by making each community's requirements clear. The RFC says there is no immediate expectation of new streams and that it is preferable that new streams NOT be created.

  • IETF stream: IETF working group documents and individual submissions sponsored by an IESG area director. Every Standards-Track or BCP RFC must come through this stream. Its approval follows RFC 2026 and its successors.
  • IAB stream: the IAB defines its own approval process, described in RFC 4845. Anything the IAB wants on the Standards Track still goes through the IETF process.
  • IRTF stream: with IAB approval, the IRTF may publish and update a process for its own non-Standards-Track documents.
  • Independent Submission stream: for documents outside the other streams. Approval generally falls to the RFC Editor, who seeks input from the IESG. The process is defined by RFC 4846 and RFC 3932.

The RFC Editor is expected to publish all documents passed to it after proper review and approval in one of these streams.
sections.eli5: Books reach the library through four doors: one for the standards-writing group, one for the board of advisors, one for researchers, and one for everyone else. Each door has its own checker.

sections.title: Technical Publication Requirements
sections.content:
The IETF, as a standards body, has publication needs beyond those of an academic journal. Each stream's community is expected to outline its own technical publication requirements, and the IAB must agree that they are consistent with, and implementable as part of, the RFC Editor activity.

The IETF stream's requirements are defined in RFC 4714. The IAB, the IRTF and the RFC Editor (for independent submissions) will each identify the applicable parts of RFC 4714 for their streams. If any of them defines other requirements, those should deviate minimally from RFC 4714, so that one technical publisher can reasonably manage the combined requirements.
sections.eli5: Every door agrees to mostly the same rules for how a book is printed, so one print shop can handle all of them.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The publication process must prevent the introduction of unapproved changes. Because the RFC Editor maintains the index of publications, enough security must be in place to stop outside parties from altering published documents.

The archive, any source documents needed to recreate RFCs, and associated originals (such as errata lists, tools, and for some early items, non-machine-readable originals) must be protected against storage failure and similar disasters.
sections.eli5: Nobody should be able to sneak in and change a book after it is printed, and the library needs backups in case of fire or flood.

items.title: IETF
items.text: Working group and AD-sponsored documents. The only stream for Standards-Track and BCP RFCs.

items.title: IAB
items.text: Approved under the IAB's own process, described in RFC 4845.

items.title: IRTF
items.text: Research group documents that are not on the Standards Track.

items.title: Independent
items.text: Everything else. The RFC Editor approves, seeking input from the IESG.
